title: Gathering Scientific Information
seo_title: Grade 4 Science: Gathering Scientific Information Worksheets (MATATAG)
standard_text: Science and technology have given us useful inventions. Learners gather scientific information by observing, measuring with standard units, recording data in tables and charts, and drawing conclusions from evidence. (summary of the MATATAG Science curriculum, Grade 4, Quarter 1: Materials)
meta_desc: Free Grade 4 Science worksheets (MATATAG, Quarter 1: Materials): inventions, measuring, recording data in tables and charts, and drawing conclusions. 100 questions with answers.
key_big: Scientists gather information carefully and record it.
key_sub: Measure with standard units such as meters and grams.
body_html:
How to think about it

Inventions such as the light bulb, the telephone and vaccines came from people who asked questions and tested ideas. Filipino inventors have made things such as the fluorescent lamp and the incubator for babies.

To gather scientific information, we observe and measure using standard units (meters, grams, liters, degrees Celsius). We record data in tables, bar graphs and charts, look for patterns, and draw a conclusion that matches the evidence.

Example

Which unit measures the mass of a melon?

Heavy things

Answer: kilograms

Example

Why record data in a table?

Easy to compare

Answer: it makes the data easy to read and compare

Common mistakes

  • Using a non-standard unit such as a hand span when others must compare.
  • Drawing a conclusion that the data do not show.
  • Changing more than one thing in a fair test.

faq.a: A test where only one thing is changed and everything else is kept the same.
To check our results and make them more reliable.

items.q: A table has the heading 'Time'. What is missing?
items.e: Always write units in table headings.

items.q: What is a prediction?
c: what you think will happen, and why
items.e: Made before the test.

items.q: Which of these questions CANNOT be answered by a scientific test?
c: Do people like the smell of eucalyptus?
Does the height of a ramp change how far a toy car rolls?
Does salt water freeze faster than tap water?
Does the length of a pendulum change how long each swing takes?
items.e: Opinions cannot be measured with a fair test.

items.q: What is the best way to present the parts of a plant and what each does?
items.e: Bar charts compare amounts; tables record results; labeled diagrams name parts; keys identify things.

items.q: Which is an observation, not a conclusion?
c: The ice in the foil cup melted after 20 minutes.
Ice always melts fastest in foil.
items.e: An observation is what you saw or measured.

items.q: Why do scientists repeat a test several times?
c: because the first result is always wrong
to check the results are reliable
items.e: Repeated results that agree are more trustworthy.

items.q: Which equipment measures how much liquid there is?
items.e: Milliliters (ml).

items.e: Opinions cannot be measured with a fair test.

items.q: What is the best way to present the favorite instrument of each learner in a class?
items.e: Bar charts compare amounts; tables record results; labeled diagrams name parts; keys identify things.

items.q: What does a conclusion do?

items.q: Ella's group and Kenneth's group get different results for the same test. What should they do?

items.q: Dennis says, 'Brand B is the best paper towel for everything.' Why is this not a good conclusion?
c: He did not use a table.
Brand B soaked up the least.

items.q: What should you do if one result is very different from the others?
c: check it by doing the test again
items.e: Repeating checks for mistakes.

items.q: A class investigates how the amount of light affects the growth of wheat seedlings. Which is the dependent variable (the one you measure)?
c: the same soil and the same amount of water
items.e: Change: the amount of light. Measure: the height of the seedlings. Keep the same: the same soil and the same amount of water.

items.q: Investigation: “Does the shape of modeling clay affect how fast it sinks in water?” Which variable should be changed?
c: the shape of the modeling clay
the same mass of modeling clay and the same tube of water
items.e: Change one variable: the one in the question.

items.q: Investigation: “Does salt water make iron nails rust faster than tap water?” What should be kept the same to make it a fair test?
c: the same kind of nail, the same amount of water and the same place
how much rust forms in a week
items.e: Control variables keep the test fair.

items.q: A class investigates how the length of a pendulum affects the time for 10 swings. Which is the independent variable (the one you change)?

items.e: Change: the length of the pendulum. Measure: the time for 10 swings. Keep the same: the same mass and the same starting angle.

items.q: Investigation: “Does the size of a parachute affect how long it takes to fall?” What should be measured?
c: the same load, the same material and the same drop height
items.e: Measure the result (the dependent variable).

items.q: A class investigates how the thickness of an elastic band affects how far it can stretch. Which variables should be controlled (kept the same)?
